source_refs.note: Book p. 220-221: 12.1.6 Theorem 1 (a)-(g) with examples, closing sentence on substitution. Book errors: (a) example 'Lim x->a 5' (should be x->1); (e) example has stray f and g in Lim f(3x+4) / Lim g(x+3). Teaching notes and our examples are ours.

blocks.text: Let \(f\) and \(g\) be two functions for which \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L\) and \(\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = M\), then
Theorem 1
(a) The limit of the sum of two functions is equal to the sum of their limits.
bold: (a) The limit of the sum of two functions is equal to the sum of their limits.

blocks.latex: \begin{aligned}&\lim_{x \to a}[f(x) + g(x)] \\ &= \lim_{x \to a} f(x) + \lim_{x \to a} g(x) \\ &= L + M\end{aligned}
blocks.text_alt: limit as x approaches a of f of x plus g of x equals limit of f of x plus limit of g of x, which is L plus M

blocks.text:
For example,
\[\lim_{x \to 1}(x + 5)\]
\[= \lim_{x \to 1} x + \lim_{x \to a} 5\]
\[= 1 + 5 = 6\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the second step the book writes \(\lim_{x \to a} 5\) with \(x \to a\) under the limit. All three limits in this example are as \(x \to 1\): \(\lim_{x \to 1} x + \lim_{x \to 1} 5 = 1 + 5 = 6\).
(b) The limit of the difference of two functions is equal to the difference of their limits.
bold: (b) The limit of the difference of two functions is equal to the difference of their limits.

blocks.latex: \begin{aligned}&\lim_{x \to a}[f(x) - g(x)] \\ &= \lim_{x \to a} f(x) - \lim_{x \to a} g(x) \\ &= L - M\end{aligned}
blocks.text_alt: limit as x approaches a of f of x minus g of x equals limit of f of x minus limit of g of x, which is L minus M

blocks.text:
For example,
\[\lim_{x \to 3}(x - 5)\]
\[= \lim_{x \to 3} x - \lim_{x \to 3} 5\]
\[= 3 - 5 = -2\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why are (a) and (b) true? If \(f(x)\) is very close to \(L\) and \(g(x)\) is very close to \(M\), then their sum is very close to \(L + M\) and their difference is very close to \(L - M\). Small errors added together stay small.
Two simple limits are used again and again: \({LIM} x = a\) (as \(x\) approaches \(a\), \(x\) itself approaches \(a\)) and \({LIM} c = c\) (a constant does not change). See (g).
(c) If \(k\) is any real number, then

blocks.latex: \begin{aligned}&\lim_{x \to a}[k f(x)] \\ &= k \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = kL\end{aligned}
blocks.text_alt: limit as x approaches a of k times f of x equals k times the limit of f of x, which is k L

blocks.text:
For example,
\[\lim_{x \to 2}(3x) = 3\lim_{x \to 2}(x)\]
\[= 3(2) = 6\]
(d) The limit of the product of the functions is equal to the product of their limits.
bold: (d) The limit of the product of the functions is equal to the product of their limits.

blocks.latex: \begin{aligned}&\lim_{x \to a}[f(x)\, g(x)] \\ &= \lim_{x \to a} f(x) \cdot \lim_{x \to a} g(x) \\ &= LM\end{aligned}
blocks.text_alt: limit as x approaches a of f of x times g of x equals limit of f of x times limit of g of x, which is L M

blocks.text: (e) The limit of the quotient of the functions is equal to the quotient of their limits provided the limit of denominator is non-zero.
bold: (e) The limit of the quotient of the functions is equal to the quotient of their limits provided the limit of denominator is non-zero.

blocks.text_alt: limit as x approaches a of f of x over g of x equals limit of f of x over limit of g of x, which is L over M

blocks.text: provided \(g(x) \ne 0\) in a neighborhood of \(a\) and \(M \ne 0\)

For example:
\[\lim_{x \to 2}\left[\dfrac{3x + 4}{x + 3}\right]\]
\[= \dfrac{\lim_{x \to 2} f(3x + 4)}{\lim_{x \to 2} g(x + 3)}\]
\[= \dfrac{6 + 4}{2 + 3} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the middle step as \(\frac{\lim f(3x + 4)}{\lim g(x + 3)}\), with stray letters \(f\) and \(g\). Here \(f(x) = 3x + 4\) and \(g(x) = x + 3\) themselves, so the step is \(\dfrac{\lim_{x \to 2}(3x + 4)}{\lim_{x \to 2}(x + 3)}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why must \(M \ne 0\) in (e)? Division by \(0\) has no meaning. If the limit of the denominator is \(0\), Theorem (e) cannot be used, and we must first simplify.
Example: \(\lim_{x \to 2} \frac{x^{2} - 4}{x - 2}\). The denominator tends to \(0\), so (e) fails. Factorise and cancel (allowed, since \(x \ne 2\)): \(\frac{(x - 2)(x + 2)}{x - 2} = x + 2\), so the limit is \(2 + 2 = 4\). Section 12.2 is all about such cases.
(f) Limit of \([f(x)]^{n}\), where \(n\) is an integer

blocks.text_alt: limit as x approaches a of f of x to the power n equals the limit of f of x, to the power n, which is L to the power n

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Theorem (f) is (d) used again and again: \([f(x)]^{3} = f(x) \cdot f(x) \cdot f(x)\), so its limit is \(L \cdot L \cdot L = L^{3}\). For a negative integer \(n\) we also need \(L \ne 0\), because \(L^{-2} = \frac{1}{L^{2}}\).
(1) \(\lim_{x \to a} x^{p} = a^{p}\), where \(p > 0\) and \(p \in \mathbb{R}\)
(2) \(\lim_{x \to a} c = c\)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: In (g)(1), when \(p\) is not a whole number, \(a^{p}\) must make sense as a real number; for example \(\lim_{x \to 9} x^{1/2} = 9^{1/2} = 3\) is fine, but \(x^{1/2}\) near \(a = -4\) is not real. In (g)(2), \(c\) is a constant: \(\lim_{x \to 5} 7 = 7\), because the value \(7\) does not depend on \(x\).
We conclude from the theorems on limits that limits are evaluated by merely substituting the number that \(x\) approaches into the function.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our example (not in the book): evaluate \(\lim_{x \to 2}(x^{2} + 3x - 1)\).
\[\lim_{x \to 2}(x^{2} + 3x - 1)\]
\[= \lim_{x \to 2} x^{2} + \lim_{x \to 2} 3x - \lim_{x \to 2} 1\]
\[= (2)^{2} + 3(2) - 1\]
\[= 4 + 6 - 1 = 9\]
Why: (a) and (b) split the sum and difference; (c) takes out the 3; (f) or (g)(1) gives \(\lim x^{2} = 4\); (g)(2) gives \(\lim 1 = 1\).
Another: \(\lim_{x \to 4}\frac{2x + 1}{x - 3}\). The denominator's limit is \(1 \ne 0\), so (e) applies:
\[\lim_{x \to 4} \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 3}\]
\[= \dfrac{\lim_{x \to 4}(2x + 1)}{\lim_{x \to 4}(x - 3)}\]
\[= \dfrac{8 + 1}{4 - 3} = \dfrac{9}{1} = 9\]
Check: substituting \(x = 4\) directly gives \(\frac{9}{1} = 9\), as the closing sentence says.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: When you use a theorem in an exam, name it in brackets beside the step, e.g. "(limit of a sum)", "(limit of a quotient, denominator's limit \(\ne 0\))". Before using the quotient theorem, always check the denominator's limit first.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Limits split over sums, differences, constant multiples and products: \(L + M\), \(L - M\), \(kL\), \(LM\).
2. Limit of a quotient \(= \frac{L}{M}\) only when \(M \ne 0\).
3. \(\lim [f(x)]^{n} = L^{n}\); \(\lim x^{p} = a^{p}\); \(\lim c = c\).
4. So for polynomials (and for quotients whose denominator does not tend to \(0\)) the limit is found by substituting \(x = a\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Substituting blindly when the denominator becomes \(0\). \(\frac{0}{0}\) is not \(1\) and not \(0\); it means "simplify first".
2. Changing the point midway (as in the book's misprint \(x \to a\) in example (a)). Every limit in one working has the same \(x \to a\).
3. Writing \(\lim\) in front of a number after substituting, e.g. "\(\lim 5\)" at the end. Once \(x\) is replaced, the limit sign goes.
